Asked about the renewed unrest inside the country, Trump offered a direct message to demonstrators on the ground: "Keep protesting."

articles.title: Opinion - Democrats are laying off many of the people who just made their victory possible
articles.summary: Following recent layoffs within its digital operations, critics argue the Democratic National Committee must maintain permanent infrastructure to sustain its...
articles.body:
After the 2024 election, the Democratic National Committee's digital operation was, in the words of one of the people who later rebuilt it, "stripped for parts."

Paulina Mangubat, the committee's deputy chief mobilization officer, wrote about it last week in the industry newsletter "Link in Bio." Much of the creator program was lost, the team was dismantled, and the work started over from scratch. So she set out to build something that would outlast a single election cycle and helped Democrats win back the internet. Then, last week, as Mangubat herself voluntarily departed the DNC, several of her colleagues were laid off.

On Nov. 2, DNC Chair Ken Martin was publicly touting the most successful social media cycle in party history: 8.5 billion views on branded content, 6.8 million new followers and nearly 4.3 billion additional views from FactPost, the committee's unbranded operation. The team built a network of more than 700 independent creators with a combined following exceeding 175 million , supplied with clips they could turn into their own content and distribute to Americans who might never follow an official Democratic Party account. As a member of that creator network, I've seen firsthand how effectively the team gets content into the hands of people who can amplify it.

Then Democrats won both chambers of Congress. Now the DNC has laid off many of the people who helped make that victory possible .

Anyone who has worked in Democratic politics knows that staffing up ahead of an election and scaling back immediately afterward is standard practice. Indeed, the DNC filed a layoff notice on Sept. 14 , well before Democrats knew the magnitude of their coming midterm victory. Many of these positions were likely designed to be temporary from the outset. My objection is not that the DNC is departing from a standard off-cycle practice, but that it is adhering to a practice that no longer makes real strategic sense. Digital communications is one area of modern politics where the work between elections is every bit as important as the work during them.

Martin faces real financial constraints. The committee carries millions in debt and a significant cash disadvantage relative to the Republican National Committee . But Martin has already demonstrated that he understands the case for permanent infrastructure: His commitment of more than $1 million a month to state parties was premised on exactly that argument. It was a smart investment. But the logic should not stop at the state funding level.

I served on Hillary Clinton's digital team in 2016 and have spent a decade watching our party treat online communication as a seasonal expense – something to ramp up in an election year, outsource to consultants and scale back before Thanksgiving.

But persuasion is a year-round endeavor. Americans increasingly form impressions of politicians and institutions in digital spaces long before anyone shows them a campaign advertisement. Republicans figured this out years ago . The conservative media ecosystem runs whether or not President Trump is on the ballot. Its personalities build audiences and credibility daily, allowing Republican candidates to enter an election year as beneficiaries of work their campaigns never had to fund.

Democrats spent much of 2025 lamenting our inability to compete in that environment. Having finally shown some aptitude for it, we are watching some of the people responsible update their résumés.

What made the DNC's operation work was distribution, not just production. And distribution depends on relationships that individual staffers spend months or years cultivating. So does the institutional knowledge that allows a digital team to recognize why one piece of content lands and another dies, or spot an opening in a news cycle before it closes. None of that is easily recovered by reposting the same job listings in 18 months.

There's a fiscal case here, too. Democrats spend enormous sums on television advertising to reach voters they have often made little effort to engage between elections. Maintaining an audience is considerably more sensible than repeatedly paying to reach one from scratch.

Martin campaigned for the chairmanship on a promise to break up the Democratic consultant-industrial complex. The Bulwark reported earlier this year that his continued spending on consultants had drawn criticism from party officials. If the committee has to make hard financial decisions, keeping in-house digital talent with a demonstrated record of success should rank as a bigger priority.

The DNC is not a campaign that just wrapped. It is the permanent institution charged with advancing the party's interests between elections. Over the next two years, Democrats will have to communicate the findings of congressional investigations, prosecute legislative fights, and make their case to voters who aren't paying attention yet to the 2028 race.

The committee should protect year-round funding for its core digital content, rapid response and creator partnership teams, expanding them in election years rather than repeatedly rebuilding them. Mangubat's team spent the better part of two years restoring what the party had stripped for parts. Now the party risks doing it again.

Between now and 2028, Democrats will spend millions on consultants hired to explain how we might better reach Americans online. We could start by keeping the people who already figured it out.

Kaivan Shroff was a 2024 DNC presidential delegate and worked as a digital organizer on Hillary Clinton's 2016 campaign. He is an attorney and senior advisor to the Institute for Education, a non-profit in Washington .

articles.title: Democrats clinch a historic House majority of at least 258 seats, the largest since 1992
articles.summary: WASHINGTON (AP) — House Democrats have secured their best general election result in decades, winning at least 258 seats in an election sweep unseen since 19...
articles.body:
WASHINGTON (AP) — House Democrats have secured their best general election result in decades, winning at least 258 seats in an election sweep unseen since 1992 that creates not only vast opportunities to govern but also intense pressure to deliver on campaign promises and priorities.

Democrats have gained 44 House seats so far, four more than the 40 they picked up in President Donald Trump's first midterm in 2018.

The 258-seat tally was reached Sunday after Democrat Chuck Hubbard defeated Republican Rep. Virginia Foxx in North Carolina. Four other House races remain outstanding: one each in Minnesota and Tennessee and two in Louisiana that are heading to a December runoff.

Republicans will have at least 173 seats in the minority.

The milestone in the 435-member House sets up divided government, with the Senate also in Democratic hands and with a Republican president in the White House. Emboldened Democrats are preparing a 100-day agenda to address high costs of living while also confronting Trump with a vast oversight agenda for the remainder of his second term in office.

The Democrats' majority will be bigger than any the party has seen in elections since Bill Clinton was first elected president in 1992 (258) or the election of Barack Obama in 2008 (257), yet not quite the high-water mark of the Franklin D. Roosevelt-era, which saw House Democratic majorities swell past 300.

It presents opportunities and challenges ahead.

"Like, hell yeah, we should feel pressure," said Democratic Rep. Jason Crow of Colorado, a former Army Ranger.

"There are people dying in this country and people losing their healthcare, losing their livelihoods, losing their farms, being terrorized from ICE," he said earlier this month at the Capitol, referring to U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement. "If you don't feel a sense of urgency and pressure in this job, and a desperation to deliver for folks, then you don't belong under this Capitol dome."

Election rout creates a mandate to govern

The numbers underscore the extraordinary scale of Democratic wins , which spanned from the strongest Republican states to the Midwest and East Coast , as voters, angry over high prices and the Iran war and concerned over corruption, made clear their discontent with Trump.

Taking control of both the House and the Senate come January, the Democrats will carry with them the backing of voters and the expectations to deliver. The Senate Democrats won a 56-seat majority in the 100-member chamber, their biggest advantage in over a decade.

The Democrats, as part of their 100-day agenda, are planning swift votes to reverse the Republicans' Medicaid cuts and restore the Affordable Care Act tax credits the Republicans allowed to expire.

Democrats have vowed to marshal their subpoena powers and launch a flurry of investigations to exert the role of Congress as a check on presidential power. That includes plans to probe how Trump and his family have become wealthier since he returned to office. Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York, who is in line to become House speaker, has not ruled out trying to impeach Trump for a third time.

"This is a historic moment for our country. This is one of the largest classes we have seen," said progressive leader Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., at the Capitol.

She called the big numbers "a mandate for change."

Rep. Tom Suozzi, a centrist Democrat from New York and an accountant by profession, said the House Democrats should focus 75% of their time on affordability issues and 25% on accountability.

"Everything should be tied back to the people — and how it's affecting the people," he said.

For example, he said, as the Democrats launch investigations into Trump's financial dealings, they should be connecting the dots: "How does that affect people's pocketbooks?"

The White House has issued a warning to Democrats over their planned probes into the administration , going as far as claiming that such investigations — a standard oversight function of Congress — may amount to "blatant criminality."

After House Speaker Mike Johnson , R-La., struggled to keep the House functioning for the past two years with a narrow single-digit majority — meaning a few GOP lawmakers could derail the agenda — the Democrats will have a wide margin that provides the new leadership much more room to maneuver.

Jeffries, who is poised to make history as the first Black speaker of the House if his colleagues elect him to the job on Jan. 3, 2027, will be able to lose dozens of Democrats on any given vote and still have the 218 needed for passage, in the face of GOP opposition.

"We're not a monolith — people come to the caucus with different ideas — it's OK," said Rep. Troy Carter, D-La., who is expected to lead the Congressional Black Caucus.

Republicans saw their number of House seats fall to one of the lowest tallies in decades. They're far from the end of the Obama administration, when the House Republicans won 247 seats in the 2014 election and the rise of Newt Gingrich when they won 230 seats in 1994.

Rep. Jim Jordan of Ohio, who was elected by his colleagues to be the Republican leader in the minority, vowed to fight their way back to power.

"Over the next two years, House Republicans will fight for American families," Jordan said.

The GOP's high-water marks include the 1920 election, with 301 seats for House Republicans.

articles.summary: WASHINGTON (AP) — Democrat Chuck Hubbard was elected to the House from North Carolina, defeating veteran Republican Rep. Virginia Foxx, who chairs the powerf...
articles.body:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Democrat Chuck Hubbard was elected to the House from North Carolina, defeating veteran Republican Rep. Virginia Foxx, who chairs the powerful House Rules Committee.

Foxx said in a statement Sunday that she called Hubbard to concede after a recount failed to close the narrow gap between them. Hubbard leads by 330 votes out of 287,000 cast.

Foxx was first elected to the House in 2004. The 5th Congressional District covers a rural stretch of western North Carolina.

"The peaceful transition of elected office from one person to another is one of the true hallmarks of our system of government, and I am proud to be a citizen of a nation that prizes fair and free elections," Foxx said in a statement.

Hubbard is a longtime journalist who got his start working for the local newspaper owned by members of his family.

"Let me be the first to thank Congresswoman Foxx for her decades of service and countless sacrifices," he wrote in a post on X.

Hubbard's victory is the capstone to a larger Democratic rout in North Carolina — and deep wins nationally — in the Nov. 3 midterm elections, giving the party control of the House and Senate when the next Congress convenes in January.

Roy Cooper, the state's former governor, won election to the Senate, becoming the first Democrat elected to the chamber since 2008. And Democratic candidates won 11 of the state's 14 House seats despite redistricting efforts that were meant to give Republicans an advantage.

articles.title: Bessent: We "need answers" on Nvidia role in sending China AI chips
articles.summary: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent says the government wants to know if Nvidia had "malicious actors down at the bottom of the company who were responsible for...
articles.body:
Washington — Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Sunday that the administration needs answers from Nvidia as questions swirl about whether it has complied with export restrictions, after revelations surrounding its CEO's alleged affairs sent the chipmaker into crisis.

"We do need answers," Bessent said on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan."

After Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia's CEO amid revelations about extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged spy, the U.S. is investigating how Nvidia may have given China access to advanced AI computer chips, despite government restrictions.

Last week, Bessent referenced a possible "culture of noncompliance" at Nvidia, questioning whether the company was "pressing these seemingly illicit sales to goose their revenues and their earnings." In an interview on Fox News, Bessent said he needed answers from Nvidia on its compliance with export restrictions within 10 days. On Sunday, he told Brennan the administration has not yet received those answers.

"We've been in touch with the temporary management, with the lead directors, with their lawyers," Bessent said. "It behooves Nvidia to move quickly on this because we want to know what the culture was."

Nvidia's CFO, Colette Kress, has taken the helm after Huang's departure. But Bessent has urged the company to bring someone in from the outside to run the company. The treasury secretary said Sunday, "We do need to see who was in charge of compliance there."

Asked how challenging it could be to get to the bottom of what Jensen Huang was doing, given reporting about Nvidia's "handshake" business approach, Bessent said, "For deals that size, there's no such thing as an untraceable handshake deal."

"There are bills ablating that movement, there are money movements," he said. "They may not be the 100-page documents, but it will be possible to understand what has gone on here."

On his call for an inquiry into whether Nvidia had a culture of noncompliance, Bessent said that it's simply a possibility that the dynamic was at play.

"We will see, and that's why I think the board is moving very quickly to establish whether this did or did not exist," Bessent said.

The comments come as President Trump has called for Jensen Huang to return as CEO of Nvidia. Asked whether the president understands the risks that Bessent has pointed to, Bessent replied that it remained to be seen "which level of the business knew about this."

"Was it at the lower levels? Was it at the middle levels? Did it go all the way to the top? And I have confidence that the Nvidia committees are moving very quickly on this and will come up with some very fulsome and robust answers," he said.

When pressed on whether he thinks it would be a good idea for Jensen Huang to return, Bessent said, "I think we have to see where the buck stops — Were these malicious actors down at the bottom of the company who were responsible for the noncompliance?" He also drew a distinction between this possible dynamic, and Jensen Huang's alleged affair with suspected Chinese spy Alice Huang .

"I think that is kind of a canard," Bessent said. "Was there a culture of compliance versus one person's foibles?"

Jensen Huang has agreed to testify before the Senate Banking Committee and will also be interviewed by House panels in early December.

articles.title: Rep. Virginia Foxx loses reelection bid after 11 terms
articles.summary: The victory for Democrat Chuck Hubbard will have local and national reverberations as it pushes Democrats to a 258 seat majority.
articles.body:
Republican Rep. Virginia Foxx has been officially unseated by Democratic challenger Chuck Hubbard in North Carolina after a recount — requested by Foxx — broke in Hubbard's favor.

The Associated Press called the election for Hubbard early Sunday afternoon. Hubbard, who lost to Foxx by 19 points two years ago, said in a statement that the incumbent had "graciously conceded."

"Let me be the first to thank Congresswoman Foxx for her decades of service and countless sacrifices," Hubbard wrote on social media. "I deeply appreciate her commitment to a smooth transition of the office and constituent casework. We may not always agree, but we both love North Carolina and the people of the Fifth District."

Hubbard's win marks the seventh seat Democrats flipped in the state this year despite Republican redistricting efforts last year. North Carolina will send 11 Democrats and three Republicans to Congress — a reversal of the 10-4 Republican majority voters elected in 2024.

The Democratic win also notches the broader party an election-year record: Having secured 258 seats, the Democrats have won their largest share of House seats in a national election since the early '90s.

Foxx had requested the recount in a letter to election officials on Nov. 17, when the margin between the two candidates was 331 votes. In her letter to the State Board of Election, Foxx cited a state law that allows candidates to request a recount when the margin of victory is less than 1 percent.

Foxx was first elected in 2004. Now 83, she is finishing her 11th term and has already filed paperwork to run in the 2028 race.

articles.title: Aber Kawas becomes first Palestinian in New York state Senate history
articles.summary: Kawas, a democratic socialist, won with 74.5 percent of the vote, championing progressive politics.
articles.body:
New York City, United States – “You have all elected the first Palestinian in New York Senate history!” Aber Kawas shouted over cheers to hundreds of Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) members at a bar on election night.

As chants of “Aber! Aber! Aber!” filled the patio of Bohemia Beer Garden on November 3, media cameras flashed against her shiny blazer, embroidered with traditional Palestinian tatreez in gold and red.

Kawas, 34, made history as the first Palestinian , and the first Muslim woman, in the New York state Senate and the state legislature. She won the seat representing district 12 in northwest Queens, home to one of New York City’s largest Arab communities, where nearly half of residents were born outside the United States.

As her speech ended and chants of “Free, Free Palestine” rang through the garden, Stylianos Karolidis, a DSA organiser on Kawas’s team, stepped up to remind supporters that she really, really had not wanted to run for office. The DSA had to “hound her non-stop” until she acquiesced, he said.

Kawas had worked with New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani when he was in the state legislature, so they knew her organising skills.

Kawas said she did not initially think it was possible to run for office without compromising her commitment to Palestinian liberation. Her victory, with 74.5 percent of the vote against Republican Han Khon To, was part of a broader tide of wins for pro-Palestine and democratic socialist candidates in the midterm elections, including Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan and Mayor-elect Nithya Raman in Los Angeles, California.

“This midterm election showed a politics of human rights that includes Palestinians is a winning platform,” said Institute for Middle East Understanding policy project executive director Margaret DeReus. “For millions of Americans, holding Israel accountable for genocide and supporting Palestinian freedom are the litmus test.”

Days after the election, Kawas reflected on the DSA’s first approach and her doubts about entering a political system she had long distrusted. In her Queens home, a poster honouring Palestinians who had been killed hung above shelves of books on Islamic liberation, the Palestinian movement and US politics. But she ran because the political climate had shifted, she told Al Jazeera.

“It felt like being pro-Palestinian was the most important thing to run on.”

Kawas’s parents were uprooted from their homes in Palestine during the mass expulsions. Her father was uprooted in 1948 and her mother in 1967. They grew up as neighbours in Jordan before falling in love, marrying and moving to the US with their infant son in the 1990s. They later had three daughters. Aber is the third child of the four, sandwiched between her two sisters. “Which is why I have a lot of politician skills,” she said, laughing.

But when she was in the seventh grade, her father was detained by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), which her mother described as a regular occurrence in New York’s post-9/11 Muslim community. His detention meant weekend visits to prison, and it left the family struggling.

“I had to work whether I wanted to or not; you have to become both man and woman, father and mother,” her mother, Manal Abu Samaha, told Al Jazeera.

When Kawas was a teenager, she said she travelled to Albany to tell her family’s story, hoping to expand opportunities for undocumented students like her older brother, who was ineligible for a college scholarship. Lawmakers seemed uninterested, Kawas recalls.

The state senator-elect credits the experience with launching her advocacy career and shaping her goals as a politician. “It’s not upending systems, but it’s meeting real, immediate material needs for people,” she said. “That’s maybe a little kernel of what got me to run.”

Backed by Mamdani and the DSA, Kawas’s campaign said it mobilised more than 1,000 volunteers to knock on doors, make calls and campaign on affordable housing, healthcare and public transport, as well as the Palestinian solidarity work that has shaped her life.

Kawas recalled that, while Mamdani was warned that supporting Palestine would end his political career, the stance instead helped him earn voters’ trust. Seeing this, she said, made her less wary that entering politics would require her to compromise her beliefs.

“I voted for Aber Kawas because Palestinian liberation is not separate from the everyday survival and basic needs that Americans and New Yorkers struggle with,” said community organiser Doreen Mohammed. “Aber Kawas’s vocal support for Palestine is what we need more of everywhere.”

Kawas told Al Jazeera she believes her stance on Palestine helped her earn trust from local leaders. Whether it can change US policy is a harder question.

“Many of us are rightfully cautious, if not outright sceptical, when it comes to electoral politics,” said Samee Sulaiman, an anthropologist at Columbia University who studies the Middle East. “Can we build and use this nascent power to finally end American support of Israel in every way? This will be the real test.”

Kawas acknowledged that a lot will depend on the political will of legislative leaders.

“The challenge, truly, is going to be the political will of the leadership,” she said. “We [the DSA] are still a minority in the legislature.”

Her first priority is reviving the Not on Our Dime! bill, which she drafted with then-Assembly member Zohran Mamdani in 2023 to prohibit New York non-profits from supporting illegal Israeli settlement activity in the occupied Palestinian territory. Rejected at the time, it is now back before the New York state Senate.

Kawas said she remains convinced change is possible, pointing to the activists who helped bring an end to apartheid in South Africa.

“If there’s the power of the people behind you, that is what you carry with you, and that’s who you’ll be accountable to.”

articles.body: Democrat Chuck Hubbard has defeated GOP Rep. Virginia Foxx for a congressional seat in North Carolina, NBC News projects, adding to a Democratic wave that is projected to deliver the party at least 258 House seats. It’s the largest House majority that any party has held this century, according to the Office of the House Historian, and four races are yet to be called. It’s also the largest Democratic majority since 1992, when the party also won 258 seats. The second-largest House majority for Democrats this century came in 2008, when the party won 257 seats. The party cemented control of the chamber not only by winning competitive races in battleground districts, but also by winning in deeply Republican areas that voted for President Donald Trump by double-digit margins just two years ago. In 2024, Trump won Foxx’s district by almost 18 percentage points, per an NBC News Decision Desk analysis. Now, Hubbard is projected to win North Carolina’s 5th Congressional District by a fraction of a percentage point following a recount that Foxx requested after Election Day. Earlier Sunday, Foxx called Hubbard to concede, according to a source familiar with the call. In a post on X, Hubbard wrote: “Earlier today I spoke with Congresswoman Virginia Foxx who graciously conceded following the results of the recount process. Let me be the first to thank Congresswoman Foxx for her decades of service and countless sacrifices.” Foxx isn’t the only North Carolina Republican who lost in what was considered to be a solidly GOP seat heading into Election Day. Democrats flipped seven Republican seats in North Carolina, the most of any state in the nation. In the state’s 9th Congressional District, Democratic Rep.-elect Richard Ojeda II defeated GOP Rep. Richard Hudson, who this year chaired the National Republican Congressional Committee. Elsewhere in the state, Democratic Rep.-elect Cyril Jefferson defeated GOP Rep. Addison McDowell. Trump won Hudson’s district by 16 percentage points in 2024 and McDowell’s district by 17 percentage points that year.

articles.title: Democrats win largest House majority since 1992 after flipping North Carolina seat
articles.summary: Democrats have now won at least 258 seats in the midterms compared to Republicans, who hold at least 173 seats.
articles.body:
The Democratic Party has won the largest majority in the US House of Representatives since 1992, after Democrat Chuck Hubbard unseated Republican Representative Virginia Foxx in North Carolina.

The race was called on Sunday, with Hubbard beating Foxx by 330 votes with 99% counted. It was one of the closest contests of the recent midterm elections, in which Democrats also secured the Senate.

The party has now won at least 258 House seats in the midterms compared to Republicans, who hold at least 173 seats, with four races still yet to be called.

Neither party had won as many House races since 1992, when Bill Clinton won the presidency and Democrats won a total of 258 seats.

Sunday's result came after Foxx, who has represented North Carolina's 5th Congressional District since 2005, requested a recount. This is allowed under state law when the margin of victory is under 1%.

She conceded on Sunday, saying in a statement: "After running a campaign focused on my track record of commonsense solutions and conservative values, I'm humbled and grateful that so many North Carolina voters responded by supporting my candidacy, even if we came up just a few votes short."

Hubbard, meanwhile, wrote on X that he had spoken to Foxx, "who graciously conceded following the results of the recount process".

He added: "I deeply appreciate her commitment to a smooth transition of the office and constituent casework. We may not always agree, but we both love North Carolina and the people of the Fifth District."

Hubbard's win, which comes after he lost to Foxx in the 2024 midterms by nine percentage points, followed a number of Democratic victories in deeply Republican districts including South Carolina, Texas, Alaska and Iowa.

Hubbard, like many Democrats running in the midterms, focused on the rising cost of living in the US during the war with Iran - a top issue for voters.

President Donald Trump himself has suggested inflation caused by the war in Iran was probably to blame for the Republican losses, as well as Vice President JD Vance.

Hubbard has also said he will also prioritise working families and small businesses, supporting public education and expanding access to affordable healthcare, according to his website.

The remaining House races yet to be called are in Tennessee and Minnesota, while two elections in Louisiana will go to a runoff in December. In Tennessee's fourth district, Democrat Victoria Broderick leads by fewer than 300 votes, and in Minnesota's first district, Democrat Jake Johnson is winning by fewer than 500 votes.

Democrats may use their upcoming majority in the House and control of the Senate to investigate conflicts of interest and other actions by the president and those close to him, while the Senate also has the power to confirm or block the president's cabinet and judicial nominations. They will also be able to pass legislation through Congress easily, though Trump still has to give final sign off for it to become law.

However, even with control of both chambers of Congress, they will still have limits on their power as Trump can veto legislation.

articles.body:
Rep. Brad Schneider (D-Ill.) said the next Congress will be focusing on using AI to improve healthcare, jobs and agriculture.

“We can make sure that we do have people overseeing and protecting American interests, American citizens from the risk of AI, while at the same time, making sure that American companies and American technologies are leading the way,” Schneider told host Chris Stirewalt during an appearance on NewsNation’s “The Hill Sunday.”

He said the Democratic agenda in the upcoming Congress should be geared at addressing the cost of living to make “it easier for people not just to make ends meet,” while also ensuring “America continues to lead on frontier technologies.”

“Using AI to improve Americans’ healthcare, to improve opportunities, economic opportunities and jobs, to improve production of food and agriculture,” he concluded. “All of these go hand in glove, and that’s what we’re going to focus on.”

On Sunday, Democrats secured their largest margin in the House in the last three decades, with many lawmakers announcing greater scrutiny into the tech industry.

Schneider leads the New Democrat Coalition, a center-left group of House Democrats focused on pro-business policies. The coalition’s working group has prioritized AI policies , particularly, that “translate into real benefits for hardworking, middle-class Americans.”

The group’s focus on emerging technologies will be expected to contend with progressives in the party who are already unveiling plans to relax the development of AI.

Rep. Greg Casar (D-Texas) said the Democratic Party “must make it a top priority to protect Americans’ jobs, freedom and lives from AI billionaires.”

“AI company CEOs should be called to testify under oath,” he continued. “Congress should investigate how these companies are putting the jobs, freedom, and lives of Americans at risk. And we should pass bills to protect people.”

In the upper chamber, key Senators are already on board with the oversight push.

Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), who appears poised to chair the Senate Banking Committee, warned Wall Street executives and Big Tech CEOs alike that “accountability is coming.”

articles.standfirst: El presidente asegura ante Gonzo que durmió tranquilo tras cumplir su objetivo de debate
articles.summary: El presidente asegura ante Gonzo que durmió tranquilo tras cumplir su objetivo de debate
articles.body: El presidente del Gobierno en funciones, Pedro Sánchez, ha rebajado la carga épica del enfrentamiento televisivo con Alberto Núñez Feijóo al asegurar que no le quedó ninguna escena grabada antes de dormir. Ante las preguntas de Gonzo en 'Salvados', el jefe del Ejecutivo defendió su tranquilidad posterior al encuentro y enmarcó su actuación dentro de una larga trayectoria en citas electorales. La conversación del 'Cara a cara' llegó tras hablar sobre las imágenes que le vinieron a la mente una vez se fue a dormir y las luces se apagaron y Sánchez respondió de forma tajante: "Ninguno. Muy previsible el debate por parte del señor Feijóo". El candidato del PSOE sostuvo que su balance nocturno fue positivo porque logró lo que había planificado de antemano para la cita. Según explicó durante la entrevista, su estado de ánimo al acostarse estuvo marcado por el deber cumplido frente a las expectativas del guion previsto: "Yo me fui a la cama con la satisfacción de haber cumplido con mi objetivo, con el que me había marcado eh para este debate". Para contextualizar su postura, el presidente recurrió a su recorrido como aspirante y mandatario en sucesivos procesos electorales. Recordó que acumula ya seis convocatorias generales como candidato y presidente del Gobierno, un bagaje que le ha llevado a medirse con distintos dirigentes a lo largo de los años: "Son ya seis las elecciones generales a las que me he presentado como presidente del Gobierno, como candidato a la presidencia del Gobierno. He tenido debates con Rajoy, he tenido debates con Pablo Iglesias, con Pablo Casado, con Albert Rivera, ¿se acuerda de Albert Rivera?, pues también con ese". Ese repaso histórico incluyó tanto confrontaciones ya celebradas como próximas citas anunciadas por el propio dirigente socialista. Sánchez enumeró a los rivales con los que ha compartido plató y a los que prevé volver a enfrentarse en nuevos encuentros: "Posteriormente con Núñez Feijóo, con Núñez Feijóo, con Abascal y con Yolanda Díaz. Vamos a tener otro también con Núñez Feijóo, con Abascal y con Ada Colau". Finalmente, el presidente vinculó esa acumulación de experiencias a una lectura propia sobre el papel de estos formatos en la campaña. A su juicio, el recorrido previo le permite separar el ruido mediático de la percepción ciudadana: "Quiero decir con esto que tengo ya una experiencia y una visión de lo que son los debates, de lo que representan y de lo que espera la opinión publicada y la opinión pública, que no necesariamente tiene por qué coincidir".

articles.summary: Hakeem Jeffries said he refuses to meet Stephen Miller, calling him a "stone-cold racist" and slamming his role in the Trump administration's mass deportation agenda.
articles.body: Speaker-designate Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., declared firmly on Saturday that he will not sit down with White House chief of staff Stephen Miller — calling Miller a "stone-cold racist" while mulling over who his conduit to the White House will be. Jeffries, who is set to become House speaker in January, made the remarks during a recent podcast interview with The New York Times, in which he discussed ways he plans to work with the Trump administration to move forward legislation for the American people. When asked whether he imagined sitting across from Stephen Miller, Jeffries firmly said, "No," and disparaged the White House official. "I've made it clear that Stephen Miller is a stone-cold racist. Why would I deal with him at this point in time?" Jeffries said. TRUMP'S MOVE FROM WILES TO MILLER SIGNALS MAJOR TACTICAL SHIFT FOR GOVERNING WITHOUT CONGRESS Jeffries, who has historically been an outspoken critic of Miller, said he cannot meet with someone who has carried out such a violent immigration agenda. "This is the architect, the architect of Donald Trump's violent mass deportation machine. And there's cruelty associated with that. There's chaos. In fact, there's death associated with what's taking place," Jeffries said. In response to Fox News Digital, White House spokeswoman Taylor Rogers defended Miller's track record. "Unlike the hardcore, partisan Democrats who refused to work with the President and blocked many of his popular policies, Stephen Miller has a track record of spearheading bipartisan efforts: public safety reform, making our cities such as Washington, D.C., and Memphis safe again, drug pricing transparency, and unleashing a nuclear energy renaissance," Rogers told Fox News Digital. JEFFRIES VOWS DEMOCRATS WON’T ‘GIVE A DIME’ TO TRUMP’S DEPORTATION EFFORTS TRUMP TELLS DHS CHIEF TO WORK WITH DEMOCRATS ON IMMIGRATION REFORM, BUT NO AMNESTY When President Donald Trump appointed Miller, Jeffries also blasted the president’s move as an "irresponsible decision" and condemned the chief of staff for his movement to "brutalize and kill American citizens," referencing the killings of Alex Pretti and Renee Nicole Good during immigration enforcement actions. Trump defended the deportation agenda of his chief of staff pick at the time, telling Kayleigh McEnany on "Saturday in America" that, "The one thing with Stephen – he was very strong on the border." "So, he called him a racist. But we had to be strong," Trump continued. "They allowed 25 million people and killers, murderers. They allowed drug dealers and rapists into our country." The president also lauded Jeffries as a "very smart" and "reasonable guy." "What he did is pretty spectacular with getting that position," Trump said. "And it’s nice – first Black person in that position. It’s a big deal." THE MISTAKE NEWLY-ELECTED DEMS ADMIT THEY CAN'T AFFORD TO MAKE WITH TRUMP AFTER SWEEPING 2026 WINS Jeffries insisted to The New York Times that his refusal to meet with Miller was "not a boycott," and expressed that he was willing to have an open communication line with Trump, just not Miller. "I think practically speaking, one, I can communicate directly with the president," Jeffries told The New York Times. "I mean, everybody seems to have his number, but the president is not a hard person to reach." Jeffries also said he can take his issues to Vice President JD Vance, explaining that in prior administrations, engagement between congressional leaders and the White House oftentimes happened via Cabinet secretaries or vice presidents. "I wouldn't say I like any of the Cabinet secretaries within the Trump administration at this particular point in time," Jeffries said, adding that he has spoken with Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent.CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The New York Democrat declared he will "maintain a willingness" to work with politicians across the aisle to get things done for the American people. Jeffries’ office did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

articles.title: El-Sayed would pass Medicare for All as ‘TrumpCare’: ‘I don’t really care what it’s called’
articles.summary: Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed (D-Mich.) on Sunday said he would pass a single-payer healthcare bill — commonly referred to as “Medicare for All” — with the name “TrumpCare,” adding that he does not “really care what it’s called.” During El-Sayed’s interview with NBC News’s “Meet the Press” on Sunday, host Kristen Welker noted that President Trump…
articles.body:
Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed (D-Mich.) on Sunday said he would pass a single-payer healthcare bill — commonly referred to as “Medicare for All” — with the name “TrumpCare,” adding that he does not “really care what it’s called.”

During El-Sayed’s interview with NBC News’s “Meet the Press” on Sunday, host Kristen Welker noted that President Trump showed a willingness to work with Democrats. The president on Saturday shared to Truth Social a social media post El-Sayed made earlier this month, where the senator-elect urged Trump — whom he referred to as “Donald” — to guarantee “healthcare for every American, from cradle to grave.”

“My job is to make sure that we’re advancing the goal to get everybody in this country healthcare,” El-Sayed, a physician, told Welker. “I ran on three things, money out of politics, money in your pocket, Medicare for All. Now, I don’t really care what it’s called. I care that the people of this country finally have the unmet promise of guaranteed healthcare in this country.”

He said if Trump was “serious about leaving a lasting legacy, there is nothing better than the ultimate Trump card.” The Michigan Democrat noted that if Trump wanted to discuss it, he was “open to it too,” as well as Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.), who is seeking a bid to become Senate majority leader in January.

El-Sayed also referred to Trump’s Truth Social post in a statement on Saturday.

“If the President is serious about meeting the unmet promise of guaranteed healthcare in this country, I’m ready to work alongside leaders in the Senate like Senators Van Hollen, Sanders, Wyden, and Warren to deliver. President Trump, give me a call. I’m happy to chat,” El-Sayed stated, referring to Sens. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.), Ron Wyden (D-Ore.) and Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.).

Sanders told The Associated Press last Wednesday that he will push for a sweeping Medicare for All universal healthcare when he is expected to become chair of the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions (HELP) Committee next year.

He said that universal healthcare is “no longer a utopian vision.” The plan would implement a universal healthcare system over four years, lower the Medicare eligibility age from 65 to 55 in year one and expand the program’s coverage to include dental and vision care, according to the AP. It would also guarantee healthcare for children up until age 18.

El-Sayed told Welker he supports the plan, comparing it to public schools in that “everybody is entitled to a public school.” Van Hollen told Welker later in the program that Sanders is looking at making “the necessary changes going forward” with his push.

“But we can make substantial progress going forward,” Van Hollen said. “And Abdul El-Sayed laid out his version. What we’re thinking about right now is having people be able to buy into Medicare if you’re 55 to 65 years old, to say that kids are covered … So, we also need to expand coverage under Medicare. So, there are lots of things we can do, and I mean big things, in the early stages.”

articles.title: Democrats secure largest House majority in election in three decades
articles.summary: Democrats have secured the largest House majority in a regular election in decades, following their notable 2026 midterm election victories in regions where they have historically struggled. According to Decision Desk HQ, Democrats are projected to lock down 258 seats in the House for the next Congress. The last time the party secured that many…
articles.body:
Democrats have secured the largest House majority in a regular election in decades, following their notable 2026 midterm election victories in regions where they have historically struggled.

According to Decision Desk HQ, Democrats are projected to lock down 258 seats in the House for the next Congress . The last time the party secured that many seats in an election was in 1992.

Democrats’ wins in this year’s elections came amid an uphill battle for the GOP, with issues like the unpopular war in Iran, President Trump’s slumping approval rating and concerns about the cost of living weighing the party down as Election Day approached.

In this year’s elections , multiple key demographics moved toward Democrats since Trump won over former Vice President Kamala Harris in 2022. Overall, the shifts were behind an expansive rebuke of the president and Republicans in the midterms.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.), most likely the next Speaker, called the Democrats’ results “ too big to rig ” in a social media post the day after Election Day.

“Thank you, America,” he added in the post.

Less than a week after the elections, Trump, who has a history of election denial , questioned how the polls could have been “so wrong.” He also raised questions about if the elections were “honest” after indicating he thought the results were valid.

“Does anybody really believe that this ‘Election’ was honest. How could the Polls be so wrong???” Trump wrote on Truth Social.

Trump suggested that a number of early voting dumps were “so large that it was impossible to win, no matter how many people went to vote” and asserted “it’s all about the machines” without giving specific evidence.

articles.title: Jeffries faces growing pains with large majority and sprawling investigative agenda
articles.summary: House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) is set to take over the largest Democratic Caucus since the 1990s, and with it, potential headaches stemming from policy disagreements and sprawling investigations. Democrats have been in a celebratory mood since exceeding expectations in the midterms and picking up almost 50 new seats in the House, returning them…
articles.body:
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) is set to take over the largest Democratic Caucus since the 1990s, and with it, potential headaches stemming from policy disagreements and sprawling investigations.

Democrats have been in a celebratory mood since exceeding expectations in the midterms and picking up almost 50 new seats in the House, returning them to the majority with numbers they describe as a mandate to pursue their legislative goals.

Still, the incoming Democratic Caucus is also historically diverse. And even as most of Jeffries’s colleagues say they have full confidence in the future Speaker, the party is bracing for fractious fights along ideological lines and territorial battles over various investigative interests .

“We got a large Caucus [and] we’re going to have to be disciplined. I mean, there will be moments. But I’m also going to say to you that our Caucus watched the Republicans, and we know we can’t perform like that. We know we can have intense discussions, but in the end, we got to produce because we got two years,” said Rep. Debbie Dingell (Mich.), chair of the Democratic Policy and Communications Committee.

“When [President] Trump got elected, they were sending a message they didn’t like what we were doing. This [election] is an overwhelming ‘they didn’t like what was happening.’ And if we don’t deliver, it’s a presidential election year, they’re going to deliver again, and we can’t afford that.”

While the election of several new members affiliated with the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) sparked concerns the left flank could stall some policy goals, the party also saw a much larger wave of moderate members win new seats. The challenge for Jeffries will be in balancing the sometimes-competing interests of those two groups without alienating either one.

Additionally, Democrats are promising expansive probes into allegations of executive corruption, with a particular focus on the president’s family and administration officials, meaning multiple committees could be competing for the same witness testimony or duplicating investigative efforts.

One Democratic aide noted that Rep. Nancy Pelosi (D-Calif.), when she was leader, was known to play traffic cop among committees as her staff helped delineate what each panel should focus on.

The aide said there is an appetite for Jeffries to assume a similar role as “a reasonable traffic cop.”

“[Jeffrey] Epstein and immigration and corruption — those are right now facing a four-way stop,” the aide said.

“And unless Jeffries stands in the middle and directs traffic on how we divvy that up, and continues those conversations on how that divvies up, it’s just going to be a chaotic mess when committees start holding their hearings or asking for the first conversations or transcribed interviews with whatever investigative targets they have.”

Democrats have already launched dozens of probes while in the minority, but they’ve been almost entirely ignored by the GOP administration.

Several leading lawmakers have not hidden their enthusiasm about their newfound power, which features the ability to subpoena documents and compel testimony — including from the executive branch.

Rep. Robert Garcia (D-Calif.), set to take the House Oversight gavel next year, issued a two-word statement the night of the election: “ Lawyer up .”

White House counsel Will Scharf has since penned two letters, one to Garcia and another to committee leaders broadly, making the remarkable assertion their probes could be criminal if done to harass witnesses. He also told Democrats they would need to start over and resubmit their requests for documents once they are formally in the majority.

Underlying that are plans for sprawling investigations with overlapping territory. Immigration is an interest already shared by three committees: Judiciary, Oversight and Homeland Security.

The Trump family’s profiting off the presidency has also already been explored by multiple panels, and Democrats have vowed to show how those in the president’s circle have enriched themselves through their positions even as Americans face rising costs.

Even the Epstein investigation, largely the focus of Oversight, crosses into other jurisdictions. Judiciary oversees the Bureau of Prisons, and both panels are probing the transfer of Epstein associate Ghislaine Maxwell.

The correspondence from Scharf foreshadows an aggressive resistance from the White House and underscores the need for coordination and strategizing a Democratic response.

But while some worry the party may cross wires, others say they appreciate that Jeffries has not been a micromanager.

One Democratic lawmaker, granted anonymity to speak freely, noted that Jeffries has avoided “punitive measures” for those who have bucked the Caucus, either on votes or in the approach they take in committee.

“I love freedom, so freedom is great,” the lawmaker said.

“They’ve, especially for committee work, sometimes weighed in, but have been very understanding and accommodating of members as they try to do things,” the Democrat added.

“When leadership has data showing that this type of wording or rhetoric is not helpful and undermines our case, a lot of us listen and take that into consideration. Do all of us bend all of the time? No, that doesn’t happen right now. I don’t think it’s going to happen in the next Congress. There’s going to be people who openly [fight] leadership when they try to tell us to do something, right? Because they don’t like what they’re saying. So that’s going to happen.”

Jeffries’s office did not respond to a request for comment for this story.

Current and former leadership said there will undoubtedly need to be some coordination on investigations.

“You don’t want to step on your own message. You want to have things relatively focused on what you want to focus on, so that you will magnify the public’s ability to see what we’re doing, as opposed to be distracted by three or four things you’re doing at the same time,” said Rep. Steny Hoyer (D-Md.), the former majority leader.

“Now, will things happen at the same time and just in the normal course? Of course they will. But to the extent you can provide a focus, I think the Speaker will be working with the committee chairs to do that.”

Almost all agree Pelosi was a masterful leader over her many years at the helm of the party.

But Rep. Pete Aguilar (D-Calif.), who will be the majority whip next year, said he has full confidence in Jeffries.

“We’ve seen his leadership style. We know it’s a little bit different. We served at the leadership table with Nancy Pelosi. She’s amazing. She’s on the Mount Rushmore of Democratic politicians,” he said.

“But this leadership team does it a little differently, and we look forward to being effective for our members.”

Rep. Don Beyer (D-Va.) said Jeffries will make “a good father in that respect” if any turf wars surface among committee chairs.

“He will — I don’t know ‘lay down the law’ — but I think he will guide them to constructive decisions,” Beyer said.

“He’s not a wallflower. He’s not somebody who rolls over. He’s very serious, very thoughtful.”

Questions linger over how aligned Democrats will remain as they push forward on policies they’ve promised to combat, such as Trump’s impact on the cost of living, immigration, healthcare and more.

The Democratic primaries saw several DSA members knocking off veteran incumbents, spurring concerns over the summer that the new “bloc” could be akin to the GOP’s Freedom Caucus, whose members routinely derailed votes and left Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) scrambling to advance even partisan bills.

The election of so many Democrats who flipped GOP-held seats now raises questions over whether the party may have trouble securing their votes on some party priorities that could be controversial in front-line districts.

“There are many times, just from political calculations, where the Speaker’s office has to drive the short-term agenda and the long-term agenda. For example, what bills do we want to take up the first and second week of January?” Beyer said.

“He’s been minority leader, so it’s different. It is different. So he’ll have a lot more power now, and hopefully use it wisely. I think he will.”

Hoyer said for all the new voices in the conference, he feels confident the Caucus is aligned on the prevailing issues Democrats campaigned on.

“I think the Democratic leadership is, and I think will continue to focus on the issues of affordability of healthcare, of housing costs, of getting this war ended, and I think that’s what they ought to be doing,” he said.

“And I think they will do it. And I think the Caucus is pretty united on those issues.”

articles.title: This Week on The Hill: Lawmakers break for Thanksgiving as year-end agenda looms
articles.summary: Lawmakers are home for Thanksgiving, but they will have little time to enjoy the break before returning to a packed legislative agenda. With Democrats set to take control of both chambers in January, Republicans have just a few weeks left to push through their priorities before the clock on their power expires. Government funding and…
articles.body:
Lawmakers are home for Thanksgiving, but they will have little time to enjoy the break before returning to a packed legislative agenda.

With Democrats set to take control of both chambers in January, Republicans have just a few weeks left to push through their priorities before the clock on their power expires. Government funding and a major bipartisan permitting reform bill are among the biggest items facing lawmakers during the lame-duck session.

The most pressing deadline is Dec. 11, when government funding is set to expire. Lawmakers must either pass all 12 appropriations bills or approve another stopgap measure, known as a continuing resolution (CR), to keep the government open and avoid a shutdown.

The lower chamber will also have to decide when to take up a permitting reform package the Senate passed last week. The legislation seeks to speed up the build-out of the nation’s energy and infrastructure. The timing of a potential House vote remains unclear.

Iran war powers resolutions are another issue to watch for when lawmakers return. Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.), a frequent critic of President Trump, said he plans to bring a resolution to the floor following his failed effort to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. Senate Republicans blocked a war powers resolution last week that would have directed Trump to end hostilities in Iran, underscoring the partisan nature of the administration’s military actions.

Meanwhile, the White House will keep up its own Thanksgiving tradition. Trump is scheduled to host the annual White House turkey pardon ceremony Tuesday on the South Lawn.

Government funding deadline looms : Senate Republicans on the Appropriations Committee are saying that a short-term CR is likely.

House to take up permitting reform bill: GOP leaders are aiming to take up the bill, which would streamline the process for approving energy projects, after the lower chamber returns from break.

Massie looking at another Iran war powers resolution: The effort from Massie comes as the Iran war has stretched on for nearly ten months.

Trump to hold turkey pardon ceremony: The two turkeys Trump is pardoning were raised on a farm in West Virginia.

House Appropriations Committee Chair Tom Cole (R-Okla.) has repeatedly said he wants to push through all 12 appropriations bills, rather than pass a CR, even as Congress operates on a tight deadline to meet the funding cutoff.

“A lame duck doesn’t have to leave full-year bills dead in the water. I’ve been actively working with my counterparts to advance negotiations, avoid an unnecessary shutdown, and get full-year FY27 [fiscal year 2027] legislation signed into law. With all twelve Senate bills now public and the House measures long on the table, we have what we need to negotiate in earnest,” Cole said in a statement last week.

“The biggest disservice to the American people would be not to try. I refuse to let any opportunity available pass us by simply because some are already looking at the next Congress while this one still has votes to take,” Cole added.

House Appropriations Committee ranking member Rosa DeLauro (D-Conn.) told reporters last week that she is in favor of passing full-year spending bills for as many uncontroversial funding priorities as possible, and a “short” CR to extend other funding.

The three appropriations bills the House has passed so far — funding military construction and the Department of Veterans Affairs, the State Department, and agriculture and rural development — represent some of the lowest-hanging fruit.

Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) is sure to face much tougher resistance, both from Democrats and within his party, when the topic shifts to funding other agencies, including the departments of Homeland Security, Defense, and Health and Human Services.

Senate Appropriations Committee Chair Susan Collins (R-Maine) released text for all 12 bills negotiated by the upper chamber this month. But Republicans on the Senate Appropriations Committee said the end result is likely going to be some kind of short-term CR.

“Everybody’s talking about a continuing resolution,” Sen. Mike Rounds (R-S.D.) said last week. “And it may be a resolution with some anomalies to it. That’ll depend, but I’m not hearing anybody talking about actually getting the appropriation bills done at this stage of the game, other than a continuing resolution until sometime in February or March. It’s just the reality of where we’re at today.”

The lower chamber is expected to take up a bipartisan permitting reform bill, called the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA), that would make changes to the nation’s environmental laws aimed at making it easier to build projects and make it harder to block them, with either lawsuits or other legal mechanisms.

“This critical legislation will cut red tape, create jobs, and lower costs for families,” House Majority Leader Steve Scalise (R-La.) wrote on social platform X. “It is more important now than ever that the House passes this permitting reform bill to the President. Now is the time to finish the job.”

The bill will likely face smooth passage in the House and garner bipartisan support.

Democratic Reps. Scott Peters (Calif.), chair of the Environment, Climate and Clean Energy task force; Brad Schneider (Ill.), the New Democrat Coalition’s outgoing chair; and Nikki Budzinski (Ill.), the coalition’s incoming chair, issued a joint statement last week praising the bill.

“BAAJA will help streamline permitting processes while maintaining key environmental protections to strengthen aging infrastructure and create over 100k good-paying union jobs. The bill also includes the toughest restrictions on data centers – requiring that they pay for their power and grid upgrades instead of passing those costs on to working families,” they wrote.

“We are deeply disappointed that amendments, including the bipartisan Manager’s Amendment, were held up procedurally and left out of this bill. As this package passes over to the House, we will look for opportunities to negotiate changes that reflect environmental and Tribal concerns,” the lawmakers added.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries’s (D-N.Y.) spokesperson previously told Politico that the New York Democrat believes the bill “falls short in several areas.” It is unclear whether Jeffries will back the bill when it is brought up for a vote.

Johnson told Politico that he could pass the bill under a fast-track process called suspension of the rules, which requires two-thirds majority support for passage. If he lacks sufficient Democratic support, he will likely have to move the bill through regular order, where GOP attendance issues could complicate passage of the procedural rule.

The bill passed the Senate last week by a vote of 62-33. Just two Republicans, Rounds and Sen. Josh Hawley (Mo.), voted against it.

Massie eyes an Iran war powers resolution

Massie told reporters earlier this month that he had filed three war powers resolutions aimed at limiting Trump’s military actions in Iran.

“If we just stay here for half the days that Mike Johnson has promised that we’ll be working between now and New Year’s, people have three chances to vote against the war in Iran. The vice president knows it was a bad move. The president knows it was a bad move,” Massie said.

“Literally everybody knows that the Iran war was a contributing factor to the shellacking we took,” he added, referring to the GOP’s major losses in the midterm elections earlier this month.

The House had previously passed three war powers resolutions. Four Republicans backed the first two, while seven Republicans voted in favor of a war powers resolution that was brought to the floor in September.

Senate Republicans blocked an Iran war powers resolution last week. GOP Sens. Lisa Murkowski (Alaska), Rand Paul (Ky.) and Collins — who have all voted for previous resolutions directing Trump to end the war — joined almost the entire Democratic caucus in supporting it.

Centrist Sen. John Fetterman (Pa.), an ardent supporter of Israel, was the only Democrat to vote against it. Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.), who voted for the resolution in September, voted against the November version.

Trump is set to hold a turkey pardon ceremony on the South Lawn of the White House on Tuesday at 2 p.m.

West Virginia Public Broadcasting reported that the two turkeys being pardoned this year were raised on Deans Gap Farm in Fort Seybert, W.Va., by Scott and Becky Rightsell.

“Out of every turkey farm in America, the President’s turkeys came from Pendleton County,” West Virginia Gov. Patrick Morrisey (R) said in a news release . “Scott and Becky Rightsell, and farm families like theirs, take care of their animals every day in every kind of weather so the rest of us have food on the table. This Thanksgiving, the whole country will see the work West Virginia farmers do.”

The People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals (PETA) wrote a letter to Trump last week calling for the end of the turkey pardon.

“It is incredible that someone in the highest office in the land can be conned every year into becoming the unpaid spokesperson for factory farmers—who have him pose beside birds bred to be so fat that they will soon be unable to walk—and get him to declare that he is issuing a ‘pardon’ to these hapless birds,” PETA’s letter reads.

The White House did not previously respond to The Hill’s request for comment.

Helen Huiskes, Rachel Frazin and Filip Timotija contributed to this report.

articles.title: Democrats win largest House majority since 1992 with North Carolina seat
articles.summary: At least 258 US House seats are now under Democratic control, with four more midterm races yet to be decided.
articles.body:
The Democratic Party has won at least 258 seats in the United States House of Representatives, its highest total since 1992.

On Sunday, a congressional race in North Carolina was decided after a recount, giving Democrats their 258th House seat, as a handful of races in the 2026 midterm elections are still being counted.

The race for North Carolina’s 5th congressional district saw Democrat Chuck Hubbard defeat Republican incumbent Virginia Foxx, who has served 11 terms in Congress.

The win was symbolic of a larger political shift in North Carolina and elsewhere, as longtime Republican strongholds flipped to Democratic hands, sometimes for the first time in decades.

Foxx was first elected in 2004, and in recent years, she was the chair of the House Rules Committee. According to The Associated Press news agency, only 330 votes separated Hubbard and Foxx as of Sunday, when the race was called in the Democrat’s favour.

Four House races have yet to be called, meaning Democrats may still expand their already sizeable majority in the 435-member House.

The party has now picked up about 47 House seats. Currently, in the outgoing Congress, Democrats hold 214 seats.

But the House was not the only congressional chamber to flip in this year’s midterm elections.

In the 120th Congress, set to be sworn in on January 3, Democrats will also hold 56 seats in the US Senate, its largest majority in more than a decade.

Those majorities give the Democratic Party significant power over legislation, although President Donald Trump, a Republican, has already pledged to veto bills the party puts forward.

Experts say the Republican Party’s drubbing in the midterm elections was driven by voter frustration with issues like the cost of living, the US-Israel war on Iran, corruption and immigration raids.

It was also widely interpreted as a referendum on Trump’s second term, which began in 2025.

As of November, only 32 percent of Americans approved of Trump’s job performance, according to a poll by the news agency Reuters and the research firm Ipsos.

Democrats have framed their electoral victory as a unique opportunity to shape the final two years of Trump’s presidency.

Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, a progressive who won her re-election bid in New York’s 14th congressional district, called the political shift a “mandate for change”.

“This is a historic moment for our country. This is one of the largest classes we have seen,” Ocasio-Cortez said at the US Capitol.

The party’s majority in the House will be larger than any since Democrat Bill Clinton was first elected president in 1992 with a 258-seat majority for his party.

It is also just above the 257 seats held by Democrats when Barack Obama was elected in 2008.

articles.title: Trump hosts exclusive dinner for investors in his declining meme coin
articles.summary: President Donald Trump will reward top investors in his declining meme coin with an exclusive dinner Sunday night as Democrats focus future congressional probes on the president’s business dealings, including his crypto ventures.
articles.body: President Donald Trump will reward top investors in his declining meme coin with an exclusive dinner Sunday night as Democrats focus future congressional probes on the president’s business dealings, including his crypto ventures. The event comes as the president’s meme coin, known as $TRUMP on crypto exchanges, has declined dramatically in worth since its launch just days before his second inauguration in January 2025. The coin’s value peaked at $74 per coin but now trades below $1. Democrats, gearing up to take control of Congress in the new year, have signaled that the president and his family’s crypto ventures will be a target of oversight investigations. Sen. Adam Schiff, D-Calif., and eight other Democratic senators sent a letter to the White House last month demanding answers about Sunday’s meme coin dinner. “This dinner and scoring mechanism appear carefully constructed to increase investment in $TRUMP, allowing the President to abuse the power of his office to personally enrich himself, as he has throughout this term,” the senators wrote. “President Trump’s continued monetization of his name and likeness once again raises serious ethical concerns, necessitating this request for a robust inquiry into the President’s financial entanglements and personal profiteering while costs for the American people continue to climb,” they added. Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., the top Democrat on the Senate Banking Committee, and Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., the top Democrat on the Senate’s Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, were among the letter’s signatories. Both senators have been sent letters from the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of Texas, Aaron Reitz, warning them against investigating Trump and his associates. The president’s net worth has increased by nearly $3 billion since he returned to office in 2025. More than $1 billion of that has been from cryptocurrencies tied to his family’s businesses, while many who invested in those cryptocurrencies experienced steep losses on their investments. Sunday’s dinner will take place at his golf club outside Washington. The White House referred questions on the event to the company that operates and sells the meme coin, Fight Fight Fight LLC. While the dinner is not listed on the president’s public schedule for Sunday, the president often holds off-the-record social gatherings at his properties on the weekends. The “Most Exclusive Dinner in the World,” as it’s described on the dinner’s website, will feature a number of celebrities, including celebrity businessman Kevin O’Leary, professional boxer Floyd Mayweather and former NBA player Tristan Thompson. The top 185 holders of the president’s coin will earn a seat at the dinner, with the top 29 gaining access to a “special VIP reception.” VIP guests will also receive Trump-themed goody bags, and the top four holders with at least 1 million $TRUMP coins are promised 18-karat gold Trump watches. Attendees, however, will not be granted a private meet-and-greet with the president, per the website. The watchdog group Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington reacted to the dinner on social media on Sunday, writing, “Trump’s memecoin dinner today, where likely unvetted $TRUMP memecoin customers will gain special access to Trump, is EXACTLY the reason why we have to ban presidential profiteering.” It’s not the first time the president has hosted a dinner for his meme coin investors. In 2025, the top 220 investors of the coin were invited to dine with Trump at his Sterling, Virginia, golf club.

articles.title: Trump criticises Schumer amid push for new Democrat leadership in US Senate
articles.summary: Schumer, who has led the Democrats since 2017, faces a challenge from Chris Van Hollen in his bid for majority leader.
articles.body:
Chuck Schumer, the top Democrat in the United States Senate, is facing backlash against his bid to serve as Senate majority leader in the incoming Congress.

On Sunday, President ⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠Donald Trump added to the ongoing criticism of Schumer’s leadership, signalling there would be tension with the White House if Schumer were picked again to lead the Democratic caucus.

“It is going to be very hard for me to work with Chuck Schumer should he become Senate Majority ⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠Leader,” Trump wrote on Truth Social.

“He failed badly as ‘Leader’ once before, one of the worst in history, and I have little doubt that he will fail again.”

The debate over Schumer’s leadership has underscored divides within the Democratic Party, particularly in the wake of the November 3 midterm elections.

Following a historic set of victories, Democrats are set to take control of both chambers of Congress in January.

Schumer, who leads the Democratic Senate minority, is hoping to retain his leadership position. A closed-door, secret-ballot vote is scheduled for December 1 to decide the majority leader.

A senator representing New York since 1999, Schumer has expressed confidence in his odds, saying he has the necessary votes to stay in charge.

“I will be elected majority leader,” Schumer told reporters last week.

But critics say Schumer, who will turn 76 on Monday, is ill-suited to lead a Senate Democratic caucus increasingly shaped by younger, anti-establishment lawmakers.

Maryland Senator Chris Van Hollen, backed by progressives, has mounted a campaign to challenge Schumer for the majority leader role.

Van Hollen told NBC’s Meet the Press on Sunday that he, too, was confident of winning.

“If you look at our caucus, you can see a huge appetite for change. They are seeing the American people and the Democratic Party calling for change. They also want to change the way we do business in the United States Democratic caucus and the United States Senate,” he said.

Schumer has also seen falling public approval ratings. In mid-November, a poll by the news agency Reuters and the research firm Ipsos found that 34 percent of self-identified Democrats viewed Schumer favourably. That percentage was down from 38 percent in February.

November’s poll also suggested that 43 percent of Democrats held an unfavourable view of Schumer, who has led Senate Democrats since 2017.

The Senate Democratic leader is the only unresolved role among Congress’s top four positions.

House Democrats last week nominated Hakeem Jeffries to be speaker in the next Congress.

Meanwhile, John Thune will continue to lead Senate Republicans, and Representative Jim Jordan ‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌will succeed Speaker Mike Johnson as the top House Republican.
