articles.title: Mamdani releases 84,000 more 9/11 records
articles.summary: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani (D) released 84,000 more records pertaining to the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks following a previous release that showed city leaders lied about air quality. “After the horrific terror attacks of September 11th and the devastating health consequences that followed, New Yorkers across the five boroughs demanded transparency from their…
articles.body:
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani (D) released 84,000 more records pertaining to the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks following a previous release that showed city leaders lied about air quality.

“After the horrific terror attacks of September 11th and the devastating health consequences that followed, New Yorkers across the five boroughs demanded transparency from their government — but were met with silence,” Mamdani said in a press release Sunday. “We launched the City’s first public portal to make these records accessible to the people who have waited decades for answers.”

In September, Mamdani’s administration released 170,000 pages of records, with the mayor’s fiscal 2027 budget including $34 million to “create and maintain” a portal where the public can access those documents.

The portal received more than 11 million visits and contained 440,000 pages, but Mamdani stated his administration’s work was not finished.

Steven Banks, New York City corporation counsel, confirmed this was the third release of records and wrote that this release marked “another step toward fulfilling the City’s commitment to providing New Yorkers with an unvarnished window into the City’s post-9/11 response.”

The documents contained city records concerning the air quality in Manhattan after the World Trade Center fell and the government response in the aftermath of the attacks.

The Sept. 11 attacks killed 2,977 people at the World Trade Center, the Pentagon and on board United Airlines Flight 93 that crashed in Pennsylvania just a little more than 25 years ago.

The 9/11 Memorial and Museum estimated that the health effects of the attacks have lingered on, as more than 400,000 individuals were exposed to toxic substances as a result of the attacks on the World Trade Center in Manhattan.

The third release comes after the Mamdani administration resolved two lawsuits brought by 9/11 Health Watch against New York City to release all of the records pertaining to the attacks.

Ben Chevat, executive director of the group, expressed in an October statement that the files showed “a disturbing record” from city, state and federal officials who he believed did not properly address problems and hazards by “slowing down a return to homes, schools and offices, or by better cleanup efforts in those places.”

He previously thanked Mamdani for being “the Mayor, after 25 years, who finally begins to answer the question, ‘What did the City know about the dangers from the toxic cloud at Ground Zero and when did it know it?’”

articles.title: Van Hollen says Democrats have a ‘generational opportunity’ in the Senate, but the party is ‘on probation’
articles.summary: Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.), who is running to become the next Senate majority leader, said Sunday that his party has been handed a “generational opportunity” with their recent wins in the upper chamber, but they are only “on probation.” “I say we have a generational opportunity because of the big mandate, the 56 votes,…
articles.body:
Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.), who is running to become the next Senate majority leader, said Sunday that his party has been handed a “generational opportunity” with their recent wins in the upper chamber, but they are only “on probation.”

“I say we have a generational opportunity because of the big mandate, the 56 votes, for change. But I also believe that, you know, we’re on probation, the Democratic Party, right? We need to earn their trust,” Van Hollen told NBC News’s Kristen Welker on “Meet the Press.”

“You don’t earn people’s trust by going back to business as usual. I think the message out of this election was economic populism. And you need somebody who has a history of fighting powerful, big-money special interests in favor of the public interest. That has been my north star,” the Maryland Democrat added.

Van Hollen , who is battling it out against Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) to lead the Democratic caucus in the upper chamber, said last week that the race is “wide open.”

“I’m the underdog in this race. After all, the incumbent has the powers of incumbency, but the reality is this is a wide-open race,” Van Hollen told MeidasTouch’s Ben Meiselas in an interview that aired Friday. “There are a lot of senators who have not declared where they stand.”

Democrats’ caucus in the Senate is set to jump from 47 seats to 56 seats in January as a result of the 2026 midterms, a nine-seat gain. The party even secured wins in states that they have historically struggled in, like Texas and Kansas.

The Democrats’ wins this year also came amid rocky political territory for the GOP, as it was weighed down by issues like concerns about the cost of living, the unpopular Iran war and President Trump’s slumping approval rating in the lead-up to Election Day.

Schumer, 75, has led Senate Democrats for nearly a decade. Van Hollen is less than 10 years younger than his New York colleague, at 67.

The Democratic caucus is set to hold its election for majority leader on Dec. 1. Per a whip list from The Hill, 6 members of the caucus have publicly supported Van Hollen, while 16 have done the same for Schumer.
